name: Ava and Hanthawaddy kingdoms (Burma)
summary: The two main Burmese kingdoms after Pagan fell: Ava in the dry north and Mon-speaking Hanthawaddy in the south, which fought the Forty Years’ War (1385–1424) before Toungoo conquered both.

location.value: Myanmar after the fall of Pagan: Ava ruled Upper (central) Burma; Hanthawaddy (Pegu) ruled the Mon-speaking south and the Irrawaddy delta.

terrain.value: The dry zone of the middle Irrawaddy valley in the north; the wet, flat Irrawaddy delta and coast in the south.

climate.value: Tropical monsoon: a hot, dry interior around Ava and much wetter delta and coast around Pegu.

resources.value: Rice, teak forests, rubies from Mogok, and good harbours on the Bay of Bengal.

disasters.value: Floods, droughts in the dry zone, famine during long wars.

population.value: Perhaps one to two million in all, mostly rice farmers.

urbanisation.value: Mostly villages and farming land around a royal capital.

migration.value: Shan groups moved into Upper Burma and took Ava in 1527; Mon and Burmese people moved during the long wars.

economicBase.value: Irrigated rice in the north (Kyaukse), delta rice in the south, and sea trade through Pegu and Martaban.

tradeRoutes.value: Merchants traded with partners across the Indian Ocean; the article names no specific partner states.

wealth.value: Sea trade brought gold, silver, silk and spices to the treasury.

moneyAndTax.value: Lumps of silver, copper and lead weighed out for payment; rice taxes and customs duties at the ports.

inequality.value: Rulers and nobles above farmers; some slavery or bonded labour.

governmentType.value: Two main Buddhist monarchies, Ava (Burmese) and Hanthawaddy (Mon), with many smaller vassal lords.

succession.value: Within the royal families, often contested between brothers, sons and vassal governors.

institutions.value: Royal courts with ministers, provincial governors and the Buddhist monkhood (sangha).

stability.value: The Forty Years’ War with the northern kingdom of Ava (1385–1424), a stalemate the article counts as a Hanthawaddy victory.

eliteConflict.value: Princes and vassal governors often rebelled or changed sides.

armyAndTech.value: War elephants, cavalry, foot soldiers and river war-boats; firearms arrived in the 1500s.

majorWars.value: The Forty Years’ War between Hanthawaddy and Ava (1385–1424), a stalemate the article counts as a Hanthawaddy victory.

territoryChange.value: Toungoo’s King Tabinshwehti conquered Hanthawaddy in 1539 and moved the capital to Pegu; the infobox gives a second fall of Pegu on 12 March 1552.

alliancesRivals.value: Ava and Pegu were rivals; both fought or allied with the Shan states, Arakan and Ayutthaya.

scienceEducation.value: Monastery schools taught reading and Buddhist texts; Burmese chronicles and poetry were written at Ava.

openness.value: Pegu was very open to foreign merchants; Ava was more inward-looking.

communicationTransport.value: Boats on the Irrawaddy and its creeks, coastal shipping and footpaths.

religion.value: Theravada Buddhism; the article describes monastic reform under Dhammazedi (year not given).

languageWriting.value: Burmese at Ava and Mon at Pegu, both written in scripts derived from Brahmi; Pali for religious texts.

artsArchitecture.value: Gilded pagodas such as the Shwedagon in Yangon (enlarged by Queen Shin Sawbu) and the Shwemawdaw at Pegu.

socialStructure.value: Royalty and nobles, monks, officials, farmers, and bonded servants or war captives.

sharedIdentity.value: Loyalty to the ruler and Buddhism; Burmese and Mon identities were both strong.

dailyLife.value: Most people farmed rice in villages built around a monastery.

neighbours.value: The Shan states, Arakan (Mrauk U), Ayutthaya and Lan Na, and the rising Toungoo kingdom.

ideasReligions.value: Monastic links: the Mahavihara at Anuradhapura, and a Lanka-trained monk installed at the Mango Grove monastery in 1361.

colonisation.value: None; both kingdoms were absorbed by Toungoo Burma.

riseSignals.value: The Mon kingdom Ramaññadesa was founded after Pagan’s collapse (1287); Martaban was the first capital (1287–1364). The article’s founder story centres on Makadu, while Wareru is named as founder elsewhere.

peakPeriod.value: Hanthawaddy under Shin Sawbu (r. 1454–71) and Dhammazedi (r. 1471–92).

declineSignals.value: Shan rule at Ava from 1527 and Toungoo’s rise under Tabinshwehti (1530s).

outcome.value: Toungoo took Pegu in 1539 (the infobox gives 1552 for the second fall); Bayinnaung re-established Hanthawaddy as a central royal seat of the First Toungoo Empire.

overallCertainty.value: Main events are known from chronicles and foreign reports; figures are estimates.
